claims.text: The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials produced using identical thermomechanical treatments.
Differences in local short-range order are the primary cause of the mechanical-property variations among the alloys.
Local short-range order alters solute-dislocation interactions.
The quinary alloy, potentially through the presence of Mn, has more extensive and heterogeneous short-range order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Heterogeneous local chemical or packing arrangements create spatial fluctuations in local stacking-fault energy.
Short-range-order-induced stacking-fault-energy fluctuations enhance dislocation pinning.
Short-range-order-induced stacking-fault-energy fluctuations stimulate deformation-twin nucleation.
Enhanced short-range order creates a rugged energy landscape for dislocation motion in the quinary alloy.
Greater dislocation pinning and deformation twinning increase strain hardening and ductility.
The quinary alloy has superior strength and ductility relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
In situ TEM tensile testing can reveal deformation mechanisms involving displacive plasticity and nanotwinning in this alloy family.
Using identical geometries, microstructures, processing histories, temperature, and strain rate isolates intrinsic atomic-level effects from extrinsic processing effects.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have less short-range order than the quinary alloy.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit fewer pinned dislocations than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit fewer deformation-twin formation events than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower ultimate tensile strengths than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will show strain-hardening behavior different from that of the quinary baseline.
A concentrated FCC solid solution of fixed NiCoCr composition can exhibit a broad range of local chemical order.
The quantitative effect of local ordering on deformation remains insufficiently established.
Failure to observe statistically greater short-range-order heterogeneity, dislocation pinning, or twin formation in the quinary alloy would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.
